","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/acc-new-zealand_we-were-proud-to-be-part-of-the-2026-fmg-activity-7480436781281153024-qTQB"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"ACC New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/acc-new-zealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-30T02:45:40.692Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/acc-new-zealand_with-a-month-to-go-until-fiscal-year-end-activity-7477552913217835008-nfse","text":"With a month to go until fiscal year end, our Turnaround Plan continues to deliver improved results. 

The monthly Turnaround Plan report for May has just been released and reflects the work our people are doing every day to ensure our clients are receiving timely, effective and fair support that helps them recover. 

One key highlight from the May report is the growth rate of the long-term claims pool, which reduced to -0.1 per cent. 

ACC Chief Executive Megan Main says this is a significant achievement, reflecting our focus on supporting people with less serious injuries, like sprains and strains, back to work and independence.

“Clients with these injuries historically wouldn’t need such a long period of support and supporting them to recover through dedicated case management is where ACC is focusing our efforts,” Megan says.

“We continue working hard to improve the things in our control. It’s about ensuring clients get the right level of support, at the right time, for their injury-related needs, within the boundaries of our legislation.

“Every day our people are doing just that, helping thousands of New Zealanders to recover from injury. But we cannot turn around performance alone. We need everyone, working together, to prevent injury and support active recovery for our clients.”

For Our Future prevention partners.

Next stops: Kerikeri and Ōtepoti.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/acc-new-zealand_little-mattering-across-the-motu-activity-7475729538816335873-JTQ1"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"ACC New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/acc-new-zealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-24T21:48:06.262Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/acc-new-zealand_for-national-burns-awareness-month-were-activity-7475666086953320448-XVg5","text":"For National Burns Awareness Month, we’re reminding New Zealanders the home can be a high-risk environment for burn injuries, but most are preventable by taking a few seconds to ‘Have a hmmm’ around hot water.

“Every winter, staff in emergency rooms help hundreds of New Zealanders who are badly burnt by hot water bottles or by having scalding hot drinks poured on them,” ACC injury prevention leader James Whitaker says.

“That's why Burns Awareness Month is focusing on these two causes of preventable burns.”

Alarmingly, our data demonstrates that burn injuries disproportionately affect young children, with ages 0 to 4 years claiming the most injuries (2,570), at a cost of $5.2 million. 

Jackie Beaumont, Clinical Nurse Specialist in the National Burn Centre at Auckland’s Middlemore Hospital, has seen a significant amount of trauma from burn-related injuries, and is encouraging parents to be vigilant as accidents can happen quickly. 

“It’s heart-breaking when you see a young child come into our centre with a bad burn injury, you feel for the child and for the parents,” she says. 

“We know one moment can have a lifelong consequence. We all live busy lives and it’s easy to get distracted. We need to slow down to think things through as most of these injuries can be prevented.”

For useful tips on how to keep your family safe this winter, head to our website: https://acc.nz/4oLryJB","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/acc-new-zealand_for-national-burns-awareness-month-were-activity-7475666086953320448-XVg5"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"ACC New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/acc-new-zealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-23T22:39:36.245Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/acc-new-zealand_this-burns-awareness-month-brayden-warnock-hannon-activity-7475316659394654210-_XET","text":"This Burns Awareness Month, Brayden Warnock-Hannon is sharing his story to remind New Zealanders how quickly a burn injury can happen, and how long the impacts can last. 

At just five years old, Brayden’s life changed in seconds when his shirt caught fire on a hot stove element, leading to weeks in intensive care and over 60 surgeries throughout his life. 

Brayden emphasises not only the immediate danger of burns, but also the long-term physical and emotional challenges they can bring.

“School was hard at times, and missing weeks for operations meant missing lessons and moments other kids took for granted. Even now, as an adult and a branch manager in Dunedin, time away for surgery can still disrupt my work and life.”

Brayden is not alone. Our data shows the most likely place to sustain a burns-related injury in 2025 was the home (15,416 claims), while the most likely cause of those injuries was preparing food or drink (3,195). 

Despite his challenges, Brayden’s shown it’s possible to build a full and meaningful life after trauma.

“The scars are part of me now. They’ve shaped who I am, but they don’t define the limits of my life. They’ve made me stronger, more grateful and more aware of what really matters.”

Brayden’s story is an example of how everyday hazards can cause life-changing injuries in moments, so taking simple precautions, especially around children, can make all the difference.

“If my story does anything, I hope it reminds people how quickly a burn injury can happen and how important prevention is, especially around children. Hot elements, hot water, hot drinks, heaters, electric blankets and hot water bottles might seem ordinary, but they can change a life in seconds.”

Read more on Brayden’s powerful story 👉 https://acc.nz/4gCEOxS","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/acc-new-zealand_this-burns-awareness-month-brayden-warnock-hannon-activity-7475316659394654210-_XET"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"ACC New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/acc-new-zealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-18T00:33:02.538Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/acc-new-zealand_survivors-have-done-nothing-wrong-but-activity-7473170879888363521-reMG","text":"“Survivors have done nothing wrong – but they end up dealing with the impact.”

For over 30 years, sexual violence prevention expert Rachel Harrison has helped organisations and communities prevent harassment and abuse – bringing deep expertise, care, and focus on what works. 

Rachel remembers being a young child when she first heard about sexual abuse – but it was during her time at university that she became motivated to do something about it. Rachel recalls her partner experiencing sexual abuse flashbacks the night before an exam, leaving them both unable to sleep. She worried about how this would affect her partner’s wellbeing, as well as her own ability to concentrate and perform well the next day.

“I started to think about how many other people in the lecture theatre of about 300 might also have been up in the night with flashbacks from sexual abuse. I thought, that’s a lot of people who can’t bring their A-game. It was like an ah-ha moment for me. I realised that, if we can’t do our best and can’t bring our full selves to whatever we choose to contribute to the world, then it’s not just our survivors who are suffering.”

We’ve been fortunate to have Rachel contribute to the development of a new initiative, Little Matters, that highlights the practical, everyday actions that help families thrive and keep kids safer.  She helped shape an approach grounded in primary prevention: creating safer environments, strengthening relationships, and making harm less likely to happen in the first place.

What stands out is Rachel’s belief that sexual violence prevention doesn’t have to be overwhelming. It starts with everyday actions. And Little Matters is about giving people practical ways to do just that.

“When I first started in this space, people didn’t know how common child sexual abuse was. Now we have more of an understanding of the problem, but people aren’t sure what to do about it. That’s why I love Little Matters.”

A big thank you to Rachel for the insight, experience, and passion she has brought to this work. 

Read more about Rachel’s story and Little Matters here:

              ACC NZ is an organisation quite unlike any other - in fact we are the only one of our kind in the world! At our heart is the fact we are an innovative New Zealand organisation born out of an idea - one focused on looking after the best interests of our people. So it will come as little surprise that a job with us offers an opportunity to do something that directly benefits the people of New Zealand, while also benefitting your career. 

There are three words that encapsulate our reason for being: prevention, care and recovery. We exist to actively minimise the chance of accidents happening. But when they do, we are here to help people with the appropriate levels of care and recovery with the aim of returning them to their normal lives faster. 

As you might expect, there are many people involved in making all this happen, and that's why there are many and varied career opportunities within our organisation. From Case Managers and Claims Managers to Clinical Advisors and Technical Claims Managers we offer many roles which open up a range of development avenues with ACC. What's more, we have locations around the country, all of which offer supportive, collegial workplaces. 

As part of the ACC's team of talented and passionate people you can also look forward to a host of benefits including flexible working options, competitive remuneration, ongoing career development opportunities, and a discounted healthcare scheme. So if ACC sounds like your type of place, let's talk today.

The monthly Turnaround Plan report for May has just been released and reflects the work our people are doing every day to ensure our clients are receiving timely, effective and fair support that helps them recover. 

One key highlight from the May report is the growth rate of the long-term claims pool, which reduced to -0.1 per cent. 

ACC Chief Executive Megan Main says this is a significant achievement, reflecting our focus on supporting people with less serious injuries, like sprains and strains, back to work and independence.

“Clients with these injuries historically wouldn’t need such a long period of support and supporting them to recover through dedicated case management is where ACC is focusing our efforts,” Megan says.

“We continue working hard to improve the things in our control. It’s about ensuring clients get the right level of support, at the right time, for their injury-related needs, within the boundaries of our legislation.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">For National Burns Awareness Month, we’re reminding New Zealanders the home can be a high-risk environment for burn injuries, but most are preventable by taking a few seconds to ‘Have a hmmm’ around hot water.

“Every winter, staff in emergency rooms help hundreds of New Zealanders who are badly burnt by hot water bottles or by having scalding hot drinks poured on them,” ACC injury prevention leader James Whitaker says.

“That's why Burns Awareness Month is focusing on these two causes of preventable burns.”

Alarmingly, our data demonstrates that burn injuries disproportionately affect young children, with ages 0 to 4 years claiming the most injuries (2,570), at a cost of $5.2 million. 

Jackie Beaumont, Clinical Nurse Specialist in the National Burn Centre at Auckland’s Middlemore Hospital, has seen a significant amount of trauma from burn-related injuries, and is encouraging parents to be vigilant as accidents can happen quickly. 

“It’s heart-breaking when you see a young child come into our centre with a bad burn injury, you feel for the child and for the parents,” she says. 

“We know one moment can have a lifelong consequence. We all live busy lives and it’s easy to get distracted. We need to slow down to think things through as most of these injuries can be prevented.”

For useful tips on how to keep your family safe this winter, head to our website: <a class="link" href="https://acc.nz/4oLryJB?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://acc.nz/4oLryJB</a></p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">This Burns Awareness Month, Brayden Warnock-Hannon is sharing his story to remind New Zealanders how quickly a burn injury can happen, and how long the impacts can last. 

At just five years old, Brayden’s life changed in seconds when his shirt caught fire on a hot stove element, leading to weeks in intensive care and over 60 surgeries throughout his life. 

Brayden emphasises not only the immediate danger of burns, but also the long-term physical and emotional challenges they can bring.

“School was hard at times, and missing weeks for operations meant missing lessons and moments other kids took for granted. Even now, as an adult and a branch manager in Dunedin, time away for surgery can still disrupt my work and life.”

Brayden is not alone. Our data shows the most likely place to sustain a burns-related injury in 2025 was the home (15,416 claims), while the most likely cause of those injuries was preparing food or drink (3,195). 

Despite his challenges, Brayden’s shown it’s possible to build a full and meaningful life after trauma.

“The scars are part of me now. They’ve shaped who I am, but they don’t define the limits of my life. They’ve made me stronger, more grateful and more aware of what really matters.”

Brayden’s story is an example of how everyday hazards can cause life-changing injuries in moments, so taking simple precautions, especially around children, can make all the difference.

“If my story does anything, I hope it reminds people how quickly a burn injury can happen and how important prevention is, especially around children. Hot elements, hot water, hot drinks, heaters, electric blankets and hot water bottles might seem ordinary, but they can change a life in seconds.”

Read more on Brayden’s powerful story 👉 <a class="link" href="https://acc.nz/4gCEOxS?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://acc.nz/4gCEOxS</a></p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">“Survivors have done nothing wrong – but they end up dealing with the impact.”

For over 30 years, sexual violence prevention expert <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/rachel-harrison-537858128?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Rachel Harrison</a> has helped organisations and communities prevent harassment and abuse – bringing deep expertise, care, and focus on what works. 

Rachel remembers being a young child when she first heard about sexual abuse – but it was during her time at university that she became motivated to do something about it. Rachel recalls her partner experiencing sexual abuse flashbacks the night before an exam, leaving them both unable to sleep. She worried about how this would affect her partner’s wellbeing, as well as her own ability to concentrate and perform well the next day.

“I started to think about how many other people in the lecture theatre of about 300 might also have been up in the night with flashbacks from sexual abuse. I thought, that’s a lot of people who can’t bring their A-game. It was like an ah-ha moment for me. I realised that, if we can’t do our best and can’t bring our full selves to whatever we choose to contribute to the world, then it’s not just our survivors who are suffering.”

We’ve been fortunate to have Rachel contribute to the development of a new initiative, Little Matters, that highlights the practical, everyday actions that help families thrive and keep kids safer.  She helped shape an approach grounded in primary prevention: creating safer environments, strengthening relationships, and making harm less likely to happen in the first place.

What stands out is Rachel’s belief that sexual violence prevention doesn’t have to be overwhelming. It starts with everyday actions. And Little Matters is about giving people practical ways to do just that.

“When I first started in this space, people didn’t know how common child sexual abuse was. Now we have more of an understanding of the problem, but people aren’t sure what to do about it. That’s why I love Little Matters.”

A big thank you to Rachel for the insight, experience, and passion she has brought to this work. 

Read more about Rachel’s story and Little Matters here: 
<a class="link" href="https://lnkd.in/eGEdyTHi?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://lnkd.in/eGEdyTHi</a></p>
